narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) for both Year 1 and Year 3, far below the average of accepted students who typically ranked around the middle of their class (decile 6 and 5.8 respectively). These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that is strongly associated with bar exam difficulty.

Your LSAT score of 38 was the third most important factor and worked in the opposite direction. This score is actually slightly above the average of 37.2 seen among accepted students, so it helped pull the prediction back toward passing. However, it was not enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.4, middle family income, and plan to attend full-time were less influential and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT or enrolling in a strong bar-preparation program that targets students with similar profiles. Many students in your situation succeed on a second attempt after targeted preparation.
